abstract: Ideal plant architecture improves grain yield per unit area in maize fields by promoting upright leaves which support high planting densities, improving light interception and enhancing photosynthetic efficiency. Shoot architecture is defined by plant height, leaf morphology, and branching pattern, which are regulated by a complex network of plant hormones and environmental factors. Brassinosteroids (BRs) are among the classic plant hormones that regulate plant architecture. Here, we investigated the functions of Cabbage (Cbg) genes in maize which are orthologs of Arabidopsis CYP90A1/CPD and encode CYP90A, a key BR biosynthetic enzyme. Using reverse genetics, we identified and characterized cbg1 and cbg2 mutant alleles recovered from UniformMu transposon stocks. Our genetic mutant analysis indicated that Cabbage genes function collectively; each single mutant (cbg1 and cbg2) was indistinguishable from its wild-type siblings. In contrast, cbg1;cbg2 double mutants exhibited severe developmental defects including dwarf stature, fewer tassel branches, and smaller, erect leaves. These defects lead to shoots with tightly wrapped leaves forming a cabbage-like head that restricts inflorescence (tassel and ear) emergence and results in loss of fertility. Consistent with impaired BR biosynthesis, cbg1;cbg2 double mutants had significantly reduced levels of downstream BR metabolites. Treatment of wild-type and single mutant germinating seedlings with the BR biosynthetic inhibitor, Propiconazole (PCZ), phenocopied untreated cbg1;cbg2 double mutants, particularly in mesocotyl elongation. Supplementation with exogenous brassinolide (BL) alone was not adequate to restore mesocotyl elongation in the double mutants. These mutant phenotypes are consistent with impaired BR biosynthesis and demonstrate that Cabbage genes (Cbg1 and Cbg2) function redundantly to regulate plant development. Overall, these findings on Cabbage genes highlight the potential of BRs for crop improvement.
